read.sections.0.heading.source: Trade links places into a network
read.sections.0.heading.back: Trade links places into a network

read.sections.0.text.source: Trade means giving goods to get other goods or money back. Goods are things people make or grow, like tea, jars or cloth. In the fictional network, the hill village sends tea by cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and Riverstone's clay jars down the river to Coastport. At this port, traders swap them for cloth and salt from visiting ships. No single trader makes the whole journey. Each person carries the goods along one part of the route. Together, these links form a network. If the river is too low for boats, traders must find another way.
read.sections.0.text.back: Trade is giving goods to get other goods or money back. Goods are things people make or grow, such as tea, jars or cloth. In this fictional network, a hill village sends tea by cart to Riverstone. Boats carry the tea and Riverstone's clay jars down the river to Coastport. At this port, traders swap those things for cloth and salt from visiting ships. No trader travels the whole route. Each one carries goods along only one stretch of the route. All these connected stretches together make a network. If the river gets too shallow for boats to sail, traders have to find another way.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Trade means giving something to get something back. Goods are things people make or grow. A cart takes tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats take tea and jars to Coastport. At the port, people swap them for cloth and salt. No one person makes the whole trip. Each person does one part of the route. All the links make a network. If the river is low, traders need a new way.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Trade is giving something to get something else back. Goods are things people make or grow. Carts carry tea from the hill village to Riverstone. Boats carry tea and jars to Coastport. At the port, people swap tea and jars for cloth and salt. No one travels the whole way. Each person works one stretch of the route. All the stretches together make a network. If the river is shallow, traders must find a new way.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Real trade routes crossed land, sea and desert
read.sections.1.heading.back: Real trade routes crossed land, sea and desert

read.sections.1.text.note: Real places in usual Thai: เส้นทางสายไหม (Silk Roads; Thai has no plural, the text says they were many routes), ทะเลทรายซาฮารา, เมืองทิมบักตู, จักรวรรดิมาลี, คาบสมุทรอาหรับ. The checker does not flag these.
read.sections.1.text.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began more than 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes, not one road, and they linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China travelled west, while horses and glass travelled east. On the Indian Ocean, sailors used the monsoon winds, which change direction twice a year. Ships could sail out on one wind and come home on the next. Ports in East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert, carrying salt south and gold north. Timbuktu, in the Mali Empire, grew rich from this trade.
read.sections.1.text.back: Real trade networks were much bigger than that. The Silk Road began more than 2,000 years ago. The Silk Road was not one road but many routes over land and sea, which linked China with Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Silk from China travelled west, while horses and glass travelled east. In the Indian Ocean, sailors used the monsoon winds, which change direction twice a year. Ships could sail out with one wind and sail home with the next. Ports in East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia and China traded spices, cloth, gold and fine pottery. In Africa, camels walked across the Sahara Desert, carrying salt south and gold north. The city of Timbuktu in the Mali Empire grew rich from this trade.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Real trade networks were much bigger. The Silk Roads began over 2,000 years ago. They were many land and sea routes. They linked China to lands far to the west. Silk went west, and horses went east. On the Indian Ocean, ships used winds that change twice a year. So ships could sail out and come back. In Africa, camels crossed the Sahara Desert. They took salt south and gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Real trade networks were much bigger than that. The Silk Road began more than 2,000 years ago. There were many routes, over land and by sea. The routes linked China with lands to the west. Silk went west. Horses went east. In the Indian Ocean, the wind changes direction twice a year. So ships could sail out, then sail back. In Africa, camels walked across the Sahara Desert. Camels carried salt south and carried gold north. This trade made Timbuktu rich.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Trade moved ideas as well as goods
read.sections.2.heading.back: Trade carried ideas too, not just goods

read.sections.2.text.note: Sensitive: "enslaved people" is ผู้คนที่ถูกทำให้เป็นทาส (people made into slaves), to keep the English focus on what was done to them rather than ทาส alone. Check it reads naturally and stays short and factual.
read.sections.2.text.source: Traders carried ideas as well as goods. Paper was first made in China, and papermaking later spread along the routes to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also travelled with traders. Timbuktu became famous for its books and teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea on the move, because a visiting trader shared a new way to decorate jars. But trade did not help everyone equally. Some traders grew rich, while others lost out. On some routes, traders also bought and sold enslaved people, who were forced to work for others.
read.sections.2.text.back: Traders carried ideas, not just goods. Paper was first made in China; later the way to make paper spread along the routes to Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe. Religions and languages also travelled with traders. The city of Timbuktu was famous for its books and teachers. In Riverstone, the potter's note shows an idea travelling, because a visiting trader shared a new way to decorate jars. But trade didn't help everyone equally. Some traders grew rich while others lost out. On some routes, traders also bought and sold enslaved people, who were forced to work for others.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: People in China made the first paper. Traders took this idea to other lands. Religions and languages moved along the routes too. In Riverstone, a trader shows the potter a new way to make jars pretty. That is an idea on the move. But trade did not help everyone. Some traders got rich. Others lost out. On some routes, traders bought and sold people. These people were enslaved and not free.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: People in China were the first to make paper. Traders took this idea to other places. Religions and languages went along the routes too. In Riverstone, a trader stopped by. He showed a new way to make jars beautiful. This is an idea travelling. But trade didn't help everyone. Some traders got rich. Some lost out. On some routes, traders bought and sold people. These people were enslaved and had no freedom.

write.example.source: First, the jar is made by a potter in Riverstone. Next, a boat trader carries it down the river to Coastport, with tea from the hill village. The places are linked by a cart road, a river and the sea. At the port, a trader swaps the jar and the tea for cloth and salt. An idea could travel when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it at home. This shows that trade can move ideas as well as goods.
write.example.back: First, this jar was made by a potter in Riverstone. Next, boat traders carried the jar down the river to Coastport, along with tea from the hill village. These places are connected by the cart track, the river and the sea. At the port, traders swapped the jar and tea for cloth and salt. An idea might travel when a sailor sees the pattern on the jar and copies it at home. This shows that trade can carry ideas, not just goods.

watch.summary.source: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road. It explains how, more than 2,000 years ago, trade began to grow between China and lands to the west. The Silk Road was not one road. It was a network of many routes that linked towns across Asia to the Middle East and Europe. Most traders did not travel the whole way. They carried goods along one part, then passed them on to other traders. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods moved along the routes. Ideas moved too. Beliefs, languages, art and new ways of making things spread from place to place. Some of these changes still shape how people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an early 'world wide web', because it linked so many people.
watch.summary.back: This animated video tells the story of the Silk Road and explains how, more than 2,000 years ago, trade between China and the lands to the west began to grow. The Silk Road was not one road but a network of many routes linking cities across Asia with the Middle East and Europe. Most traders didn't travel the whole way; they carried goods one stretch, then passed them to other traders. Silk, spices, horses and many other goods travelled along these routes. Ideas travelled too: beliefs, languages, art and new ways of doing things spread from place to place. Some changes still affect how people live today. The video calls the Silk Road an early "World Wide Web", because it connected many people together.
